Universes that grow their own space

A research page of the imigraph project (2026-11-27). Every picture is drawn from runs of the project's own rewriting engine; nothing here is a sketch.

In the Wolfram Physics Project the whole world is a heap of nodes (things with no properties, only a number) and relations between them (lists of nodes, the project's hyperedges). A rule says: wherever this little pattern is found, replace it with that one. Each replacement is one change (the project's event). Nothing is placed anywhere: there is no grid, no distance, no clock. Space, if it appears, is only who is linked to whom; near means few hops along relations, far means many.

The pictures below put every node at one place, worked out once from the last state of the run. Nodes that do not exist yet are simply not drawn, so the picture never jumps: it fills in. Grey-blue lines are relations, faint triangles are relations of three nodes, orange is what the last step made. Drag a 3D picture to turn it; nothing turns by itself.

What here is like physics, and what is not

  • Like physics: some rules grow a web in which the number of nodes within r hops grows like r² (a sheet) or nearly r³ (a solid), although no dimension was put in. A random walker on such a web comes back as often as on a sheet. A change can only influence what is linked to it, so influence spreads at most a fixed number of hops per step: a speed limit.
  • Not like physics (yet): the counts settle near 2 or 3 only roughly and only for some rules; most rules grow trees, threads or hubs. No measured world here has curvature that one could call a sphere with confidence. Nothing here has mass, charge or energy.
  • Put in by hand: the marker (a relation of one node) and the three small rules that move it are ours; the rules that grow space are from the Registry of Notable Universes. The ring with the kink is in the start, as the technical introduction gives it.
  • Made by the rule: the shape of space, its dimension, and the movement of the kink. In no world here do both the space and something that moves through it come from the rule alone.

Space, particle, movement: who makes what

Three cases were found, here and in the sources read for this page:

  • The rule makes space, the particle is put in by hand. Rules of the Wolfram Physics Project grow sheets and surfaces (scenes 1 and 3); a marker of our own is added and moved by rules of our own (scene 2).
  • Space is put in by hand, the rule makes the particles. This project's Game of Life and Bounce Gas played as Wolfram models: the grid is in the start; a glider of Life stays 5 cells and moves one cell diagonally every 4 generations, a Bounce Gas 3D particle one cell a step. Rule 110, Wolfram's own stand-in for particles, is of this kind too.
  • Space and particle in the start, the movement by the rule: the ring with a kink from the technical introduction (scene 4). The rule rewrites the whole ring in every step; the kink is the one irregular place and moves back one node per step. It keeps its shape only in the standard order of changes: in random order it fell apart in 4 of 5 runs.

No rule is known, here or in the sources, that makes both the space and something lasting that moves through it.

Four claims of another AI, checked

  • A pair of a node with 5 and a node with 7 neighbours moving like a zipper through a mesh of triangles (a Wolfram Summer School post): not found in three searches. Such pairs are real defects of crystals; the nearest Wolfram work (Chester, 2021) puts a defect into a flat sheet by a changed rule applied once, and does not show it moving.
  • A small knot that cannot be drawn flat (K5 or K3,3) in a flat mesh, kept by rules that keep flatness: partly right. The idea is Wolfram's (A New Kind of Science, chapter 9, and the technical introduction), but no such rule is given or run there; a Winter School project of 2021 (Fischer) put the knot in by hand and searched for rules, with "promising preliminary results".
  • A ring with a ripple that moves round it, in the technical introduction: confirmed: the kink of scene 4, measured here.
  • Rule 110 gliders as Wolfram's stand-in for particles: confirmed (technical introduction, Elementary Particles).

1. Space grows (a flat picture)

One change per step: the rule finds one place, removes two relations of three nodes and puts three back, with one new node. Step through and watch where the sheet grows. Switch the placing to see how much the picture depends on it: stress makes drawn distance follow hops, waves uses the slowest vibrations of the web, forces lets linked nodes pull and all nodes push (the project's own way).

2. A marker moves through it

A marker is a relation of one node, {m}. Three small rules move it to the next node of a relation of three that holds it. With the trail on, the line shows where it has been (its world line seen from above). The causal graph beside it (the project's causal graph) shows every change as a dot, earlier ones higher up, placed left to right by where in space they happened; a line joins a change to an earlier one whose result it used; the marker's own changes are coloured. On the fixed sheet, move it yourself rings every node the rules allow the marker to hop to next; tapping one picks that change. Which change happens first is exactly what the order of changes decides.

3. Curved and crumpled universes (3D)

Some rules grow webs that cannot lie flat: a flat drawing has hundreds of crossing lines. Placed in three dimensions they show a shape. Drag to turn. Switch hops from a node on and tap one of the ringed nodes: every node is coloured by how many hops it is away, and the chart counts the nodes at each distance. How fast that count grows is the dimension estimate: like r for a line, r² for a sheet, r³ for a solid.

4. Movement in time: world lines

Here every state is drawn as one layer and later states lie higher up, so time is the height and movement becomes a slanted line. The top layer is the state of the step shown (the count below counts its relations); the earlier states stay drawn below it. The first picture is the technical introduction's own example of a particle: a ring where the rule rewrites every place in every step, and one irregular spot (the kink) that keeps its shape and moves. The last picture is a random walk on a grown surface: the same marker rules, the changes taken in random order.

How these pictures were made

The runs, the places of the nodes, the causal graphs and the hop counts are computed in Python with the engine of experiments/wolfram-physics by research/physics-like-universes/build_page.py; this page only draws them. The measurements behind the text are in research/physics-like-universes/2026-11-27-universes-space-and-motion.md.
